01 / General

The basics

What Lingo is, what it does to your database, and what it deliberately does not do.

A multilingual layer for WordPress. Lingo keeps one canonical post and stores every language in a compact side table, keyed by field and language code. You get per-field translation, clean /{code}/ URLs and automatic hreflang — without a translation-management suite sitting on top of your site.

No. Lingo is standalone, with its own storage and its own APIs. It can import from WPML, Polylang, qTranslate-XT and TranslatePress, but it never depends on any of them at runtime.

No. That is the whole point. One canonical post keeps its ID; the translations live beside it. Your post lists, permalinks and admin stay exactly as long as they are today, whether you run two languages or eight.

No — Lingo is a translation layer, not a translation engine. You or your translator write each language; Lingo stores it, routes it and serves it. Copy from default drops your source text into the target language as a starting point so you are never staring at an empty field.

No. Lingo is self-hosted. Your translations sit in your own database and no external service sits in the request path. If you ever leave, the data is still yours to take.

The free version covers one additional language, with the complete translation engine behind it — nothing is crippled. Paid plans lift the cap to unlimited languages.

02 / Migration

Moving in

Preview it, apply it, undo it. Nothing about switching should feel like a leap.

WPML, Polylang, qTranslate-XT and TranslatePress. Each has its own importer, so the mapping follows how that plugin actually stored your translations.

Low, by design. Run the dry-run first — it is free and writes nothing. Apply when the numbers look right. Undo whenever you want. Your original content is never destroyed at any step.

Every post and every language Lingo would bring across, before a single row is written:

wp lingo wpml-dryrun → then wp lingo wpml-migrate when you are ready.

Your translated titles, content and excerpts, custom fields, taxonomy terms and descriptions, and media text — mapped onto the canonical post they belong to, with their language assignments intact.

Yes. The undo reverses what the migration wrote into Lingo. Whatever your old plugin stored is left where it was, so you can go back, adjust and run it again.

Only while you are checking the result. Once the front end looks right in every language, the old plugin can be deactivated — Lingo does not read from it after the import.

03 / SEO & URLs

Search, kept safe

Clean routes and correct alternates, ready before your first translation ships.

Your default language stays at the root — example.com/about/ — and every other language sits under its code: example.com/fr/about/. No query strings, no subdomains to set up.

Yes — hreflang alternates plus x-default are emitted for you. There is no annotation step and nothing to maintain by hand when you add a language.

No. Each language has its own URL and the alternates are declared, which is exactly the signal search engines look for. One canonical structure, several language versions.

Yes. Titles and meta resolve per language, so the SEO plugin you already use keeps working instead of being replaced.

Yes — slugs are translatable per language, so a French reader gets a French URL rather than an English one wearing a /fr/ prefix.

04 / Editing

Writing & translating

Lingo lives inside the block editor. There is no second workspace to learn.

In the post you are already editing. A Language (Lingo) panel switches the editing language, and the editor keeps behaving like the editor — same blocks, same shortcuts, same preview.

Titles, content and excerpts; custom fields, including ACF and plain meta; taxonomy terms and their descriptions; and media alt text and captions. Translate what needs translating and leave the rest alone.

Your source-language content is never overwritten by a translation. Copy from default only ever copies into the language you are working on.

Core blocks translate as ordinary post_content and render through WordPress's own block pipeline — no parallel renderer, no block-by-block mapping table.

Through a simple string registry. A pll__ / icl_ compatibility shim keeps themes that were built for Polylang or WPML working after you migrate, so you are not rewriting template code on day one.

Wherever your theme has room: the [lingo_switcher] shortcode, a widget, a Language Switcher block, language items in Appearance → Menus, or the lingo_language_switcher() template tag. List, inline or dropdown styles.

05 / WooCommerce

Selling in every language

Built in, not bolted on — no separate commerce add-on to license.

No. WooCommerce translation is part of the paid plans rather than a separate purchase.

Product titles and descriptions, product categories, and variation attribute values — the copy a customer actually reads before deciding.

Yes — the whole journey stays under the same language prefix, from /fr/shop through cart and checkout to the customer account.

No, and it does not pretend to. Lingo translates content and routes URLs; pricing and currency stay with WooCommerce and whichever currency extension you already run.

06 / Plans & support

Buying & getting help

What each plan covers, how updates arrive, and where the developer surface is.

One additional language and the complete core: per-field translation, clean URLs, automatic hreflang, the switcher, and the migration preview with undo. It is the honest on-ramp, not a demo.

Unlimited languages, one-command migration (applying it, not just previewing it), WooCommerce product translation, and priority support with automatic updates.

Business covers five sites at $129 a year. Agency is $199 a year with unlimited site activations — the one to take if multilingual is a normal part of what you hand over to clients.

Yes — there is a 7-day money-back guarantee on the paid plans. And you can run the free version for as long as you like before you decide.

Yes. Your translations live in your own database, so moving between plans is a licence change — never a content migration.

Through the normal WordPress updates screen. Paid updates are self-hosted and integrity-checked, so there is no separate dashboard to log into and nothing new to teach a client.

Yes: WP-CLI commands, language resolution over the REST API, and a documented set of hooks and filters. Automate the boring parts and leave the rest to the editors.
